Mem0 offers background memory consolidation for AI agents.
Mem0 provides persistent memory across chat sessions.
Mem0 targets multi-level memory across user, session, and agent state
Distinguishes between agent memory and user memory extraction, using separate prompts for each
Mem0 is described as a memory-layer idea for AI applications
Mem0 search lets agents retrieve relevant memories using natural-language questions
Mem0 stores memories scoped by identifiers and can extract, update, or delete facts across sessions using a single LLM pipeline.
Adds persistent, self-improving memory to AI apps, available as a managed platform or self-hosted open source.
Provides long-term memory that persists across sessions, tools, and runs for AI agents.
Mem0 is a memory layer for LLM agents providing persistent, self-improving context across sessions
Platform for richer add/search/update/delete memory flows with metadata, rerankers, and per-request controls
Mem0 is used to provide per-user long-term memory in web applications, with methods to add, search, and retrieve memories scoped by user_id.
Mem0 is described as framework- and platform-agnostic, deployable as a managed platform, self-hosted package, or local MCP server.
Mem0 provides a managed AI memory layer that handles extraction, retrieval, and preference updates so agents remain consistent over time.

mechanisms.text: Mem0 uses an infer parameter (infer=True vs infer=False) that controls whether facts are extracted and stored from conversation.
Mem0 uses embeddings as part of its memory mechanism.
Mem0 claims significant token/context footprint reduction via its memory approach.
Mem0 supports shared memory for coding agents across services and repositories, suggesting cross-agent or cross-session isolation scope.
Mem0 claims cost reduction through its memory approach combined with reasoning tokens.
Temporal reasoning ranks the right dated memory instance for queries about current state, past events, and upcoming plans
Managed platform includes proprietary optimizations not present in the open-source SDK; retrieval budget is top_200
Message log vs curated memory: raw conversation messages are saved to a separate history/db store (saveMessages), while LLM-extracted facts are what get persisted as memories in the vector store.

Delete path: removes the vector from the vector store, records a DELETE history entry with the previous value, and removes the memory ID from any entity store records (deleting entity records that become empty).
Expiration: memories carry an expiration_date in payload; expired memories are filtered out of search and getAll results by default, with opt-in showExpired flag.
This implementation is in-process (RAM only); the close() method is a no-op with an explicit comment confirming no durable storage is involved.
Write path: messages (str, dict, or list of dicts) are posted to /v3/memories/add/ to persist new memories
History of a specific memory retrievable via /v1/memories/{id}/history/
Isolation by entity type: memories are scoped to user_id, agent_id, app_id, or run_id; entity params must be passed as filters, not top-level
Individual memory units can be permanently deleted by ID.
Retrieve uses hybrid scoring: semantic vector search combined with BM25 keyword search, plus per-memory entity boost, filtered by a threshold before returning top_k results.
Memory delete removes the vector from the vector store, writes a DELETE event (is_deleted=1) to SQLite history, and strips the memory id from any entity records.
Expired memories are hidden from search and get_all at retrieval time by checking expiration_date in payload; they are not physically deleted unless show_expired=True is passed.

Mem0 maintains two distinct SQLite tables: a curated 'history' table tracking memory-level add/update/delete events, and a 'messages' table storing the raw conversation log per session scope. These are separate stores.
The messages table enforces a rolling window of at most 10 messages per session scope; older messages are evicted on write.
Isolation: telemetry filters encode user_id, agent_id, and run_id — indicating memory is scoped per user, agent, and run/session
Separate legacy extraction prompt path preserved for backward compatibility, implying the extraction prompt (and thus write schema) has evolved
Long-term retention by default; data retained indefinitely unless instructed otherwise, unlike prompt caching which clears after 5 minutes
Developer-reported community concern: exclusion of sensitive data relies on LLM instruction-following, not hard filtering
LLM-based extraction: messages are sent through an LLM that pulls out key facts, decisions, or preferences to remember.
Additive storage: new memories are added without overwriting or deleting existing memories.
Isolation is per user_id, agent_id, and run_id; user_id scoping prevents cross-contamination
Platform v3 uses Temporal Reasoning internally for time-aware queries while preserving normal search response shape
Memory is scoped per entity: user, agent, app, or run
Portable agent plugin provides search and skills but no automatic capture; its remember skill cannot save a new memory on its own
Update: a retrieved memory can be updated inline by memory_id with new text
Delete: memories can be deleted scoped to a single entity id (user_id or run_id); combining more than one entity filter in the same delete_all call is not guaranteed to AND them
Memory operations are performed via AsyncMemory client methods: add(), search(), and get_all(), each scoped to a user via user_id.

Memories are stored as objects in a vector store (Weaviate) and listed via a fetch_objects method; the list method does not currently pass a sort parameter, defaulting to ascending order by created_at.
Stale entity relationships from failed cleanup can surface in later search and entity-boost flows, affecting retrieval
Retrieval uses a combination of semantic search, BM25, and entity matching to rank candidate memories.
Retrieval scoring does not incorporate recency, allowing stale facts to rank above newer ones.
_upsert_entity merges a new memory_id into an existing entity's linked_memory_ids when similarity >= 0.95, without verifying the matched entity's scope matches the new memory's scope.
Optional inclusion of change history and recent session messages alongside memory facts
Hosted platform export is lossy (schema-reshaped), has no import, and expires after 7 days — a gap relative to core SDK users
When entity store isolation fails, extracted entities appear in getAll() and search() results as if they were real memories, and can rank above them in search.
Mem0 applies user_id, agent_id, and run_id as isolation filters at retrieval time; some filters are applied server-side and remaining metadata filters client-side.
Elasticsearch vector store maps only three metadata fields as keyword type; all other custom metadata keys fall through to dynamic mapping as analyzed text fields
delete_all removes memories from an entity store that tracks linked_memory_ids per scope, listing up to 10,000 entity rows per deletion in the sync path
The async delete_all skips per-memory entity cleanup and instead clears the entity store once in bulk after all deletions
Entity store cleanup is scoped (filtered), implying isolation by some scope identifier (user, agent, or session)
search() and get_all() require entity parameters inside a filters dict, not as top-level keyword arguments; top-level entity params raise ValueError
The OpenSearch vector store silently drops enhanced metadata filters, causing search to run unfiltered and return results that violate the filter
POST /generate-instructions calls the LLM directly on every request with no persistence

Auto-Recall: before the agent responds, memories matching the current message are retrieved and injected directly into context — long-term memories first, then session memories — with no manual memory_search call required.
Session memory (short-term) is scoped to the current conversation using Mem0's run_id parameter and does not carry forward indefinitely.
memory_update preserves history when updating a memory's text in place.
The ADD-only architecture means older facts are preserved rather than overwritten, which can cause a semantically similar prior fact to surface alongside a newer one (a known trade-off).
Mem0 uses priority scoring and contextual tagging to filter what gets stored, avoiding memory bloat.
Mem0 implements dynamic forgetting by decaying low-relevance entries over time rather than treating memory as a static store.
Mem0 moves information between short-term and long-term memory storage based on usage patterns, recency, and significance.
Mem0 maintains relevant context across sessions, devices, and time periods rather than resetting at session end.
Mem0 can be self-hosted inside a private VPC so that memory data never leaves the operator's own infrastructure.
Mem0 extracts discrete facts from conversational input rather than storing raw chunks, making memory more usable for the LLM.
Retrieval is semantic search via m.search(), filtering by user_id to return only relevant memories for the current query.
On conflict, Mem0 updates the existing memory rather than appending a duplicate, and preserves the context of the change (versioned changelog).
Isolation is per user_id for long-term memory and per session_id for short-term memory; these are distinct scopes.
Default write path is extraction of discrete updateable facts, not summarization of conversation history into prose
Managed platform includes proprietary optimizations not available in the open-source SDK
Temporal reasoning classification happens at write time, keeping latency flat
